title: 9 best Render alternatives in 2026, compared
summary: Compare 9 Render alternatives for 2026, including Railway, Fly.io and AWS, on pricing, databases, regions and how much operating work they leave to you.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


## Key takeaways


-


Render charges for a workspace plan (Hobby free, Pro $25 and Scale $499 a month) plus a fixed price per service, starting at $7 a month for 0.5 CPU and 512 MB.


-


Render runs in five regions, Oregon, Ohio, Virginia, Frankfurt and Singapore, and a service can't move to another region once created.


-


Railway is the closest like-for-like Render alternative, running services, workers, cron jobs and databases from a repo and billing CPU and memory by the second.


-


Fly.io added a $4-a-month Managed Postgres plan on November 23, 2026, and new Fly.io accounts start on a Free plan.


-


Modelence is a Render alternative with managed MongoDB, PostgreSQL and Redis, sandbox and production environments, and deploys from coding agents, running on AWS in 17 regions.


Ask AI about this post:


The best Render alternatives in 2026 are Railway for the closest like-for-like move with usage-based billing, Fly.io for running close to users in many regions, and Modelence or AWS ECS Express Mode when you need the app and its data on AWS in a specific region. Five more options cover narrower needs, such as running inside your own cloud account, staying on a long-established platform or self-hosting on your own servers. This guide compares each alternative to Render on pricing, databases and regions, along with the tradeoff you take on with each, using prices checked on November 25, 2026.


## Why teams look for Render alternatives


Render is a good default for getting web services, workers, cron jobs and a Postgres database running from a Git repo, and it keeps shipping, with Workflows for durable background tasks, cheaper large Key Value plans and Sandboxes in beta this year. Teams that move on usually do so because the app has grown into requirements Render doesn't fit as well:


- **Regions.** Render runs in five regions: Oregon, Ohio and Virginia in the US, plus Frankfurt and Singapore. There is no region in Canada, the UK, South America, Australia or Japan, and a service can't move to another region, so changing regions means recreating it. Render's private network also stays within one region.
- **Pricing steps.** You pay for a workspace plan (Hobby is free, Pro is $25 a month and Scale is $499 a month) and then a fixed price for each service's compute plan. The steps are $7 a month for 0.5 CPU and 512 MB, $25 for 1 CPU and 2 GB and $85 for 2 CPU and 4 GB, so a service that outgrows 512 MB of memory more than triples in price. Bandwidth beyond the plan allowance (5 GB on Hobby, 25 GB on Pro) costs $0.15 per GB.
- **Compliance costs.** Render signs a HIPAA BAA only on Scale and Enterprise, and HIPAA workspaces pay a 20% fee on all usage and can't use the Singapore region.
- **Free tier limits.** Free web services spin down after 15 minutes without traffic, and free Postgres databases expire after 30 days.


For a detailed look at the most common switch, our[Railway vs Render comparison](https://modelence.com/compare/railway-vs-render) covers billing, workers, cron jobs, Postgres and regions side by side, with what a small app costs on each.

## The 9 best Render alternatives in 2026


### 1. Modelence


Modelence is a Render alternative with managed MongoDB, PostgreSQL and Redis, sandbox and production environments, and deploys from coding agents. It runs your services, databases and scheduled jobs on AWS and keeps operating them after the deploy. An app is described in one` modelence.config.json` file, which can hold several services, such as a web app, an API built from its own Dockerfile in any language and a background worker, along with their databases and secrets. Your coding agent, whether that is Claude Code, Cursor or Codex, can write that file by reading` modelence.com/skill.md` and run the first deploy, which creates everything in the AWS region you choose and passes the connection strings to the app. The[deployment overview](https://modelence.com/platform/deployment) shows how the config file works, and the[deploy guides](https://modelence.com/deploy) walk through stacks like[Node.js](https://modelence.com/deploy/nodejs) and[any app with a Dockerfile](https://modelence.com/deploy/docker) .


**Best for:** teams that like Render's push-and-run workflow, need the app and its data on AWS in the region their customers expect, and would rather not be the ones watching it around the clock.


**How it runs your app:** every app gets a sandbox and a production environment, so you can try changes on real infrastructure before they reach users. A new version starts next to the running one and takes traffic only once it passes health checks, and a version that keeps crashing is rolled back automatically. On Pro and above, production autopilot operates the app 24/7: when a process crashes or traffic climbs, it restarts the process, reroutes traffic or adds capacity, then sends you a report of what happened. Problems that need a code change, like a memory leak or a slow query, are traced to where they start in your code. The[monitoring page](https://modelence.com/platform/monitoring) covers this in more detail.


**Databases:** managed PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Redis, created in the same region as the app on the first deploy. Production databases fail over to a healthy machine automatically and are snapshotted at least every six hours on every plan, with encrypted snapshots kept on a rolling schedule for up to 12 months. See[managed databases](https://modelence.com/platform/database) .


**Regions:** 17 AWS regions across the Americas, Europe and Asia Pacific, including Montreal, London, São Paulo, Tokyo and Sydney. Containers run on AWS Fargate across two availability zones, data is encrypted at rest and in transit, and production services run to a 99.9% uptime target with a public status page. Secrets are viewable in the dashboard, and every view is logged. For healthcare apps, Modelence signs BAAs on the Enterprise plan.


**Pricing:** free for hobby projects. Starter is $20 a month, Pro is $100 a month and Scale is $500 a month, and each paid plan includes its price in cloud usage, so the bill stays at the plan price unless your apps use more than it covers. There is no per-seat charge, and the smallest instance (0.25 vCPU, 0.5 GB) costs about $9 a month. See[pricing](https://modelence.com/pricing) .


**Portability:** Modelence runs on standard AWS primitives, so if you later build your own DevOps team, you can replicate the setup in your own AWS account.


### 2. Railway


Railway is the platform most similar to Render. It runs web services, workers and cron jobs from a Git repo or a Dockerfile, with databases deployed from templates next to them, and its main difference is billing by usage instead of by instance size.


**Best for:** apps whose load comes and goes, where paying for the CPU and memory actually used beats a fixed instance price.


**Pricing:** a Free plan includes $1 of usage a month, Hobby is $5 a month and Pro is $20 a month per workspace, and each plan's price counts toward usage. Compute is billed by the second at about $20 per vCPU and $10 per GB of memory a month, and egress costs $0.05 per GB, a third of Render's overage rate.


**Databases:** Postgres, MySQL, Redis and MongoDB from templates, each with a high-availability variant with automatic failover, and point-in-time recovery for Postgres and MySQL. Volumes cost $0.15 per GB a month.


**Regions:** four, in California, Virginia, Amsterdam and Singapore.


**Tradeoff:** Railway has no load-based horizontal autoscaling, so you set replica counts by hand, and it offers an uptime SLA only on Enterprise. Config as code is also changing: Railway stops reading` railway.json` and` railway.toml` on December 1, 2026, in favor of a TypeScript file at` .railway/railway.ts` . In October 2026, Railway[reported a security incident](https://blog.railway.com/p/incident-report-october-security-incident) in which an attacker decrypted environment variables in up to 1.85% of workspaces, and it now runs each build in its own short-lived VM. Our[Railway alternatives guide](https://modelence.com/compare/railway-alternatives) covers the other direction.


### 3. Fly.io


Fly.io runs your app as lightweight virtual machines, called Machines, on its own hardware, and makes it easy to place them near your users.


**Best for:** latency-sensitive apps with a global user base, and teams comfortable working closer to the infrastructure.


**Pricing:** new accounts start on a Free plan, which covers $5 of usage a month once a card is added, for up to three Machines. After that it is pay as you go with no monthly fee: a shared-cpu-1x Machine with 256 MB costs $2.19 a month in Ashburn, and with 1 GB $6.70. Outbound data is $0.02 per GB in North America and Europe and more elsewhere.


**Databases:** Fly Managed Postgres added a $4-a-month Developer plan on November 23, 2026, with a primary and a standby. It pauses after 15 minutes without a client and has no point-in-time restore, so production databases usually start on the $38 Basic plan with 1 GB. Every plan includes high availability and automated backups. Redis comes through Upstash, pay as you go from $0.20 per 100,000 requests or fixed plans from $10 a month.


**Regions:** regions on six continents, including Toronto, Sydney and Johannesburg.


**Tradeoff:** scheduled Machines run on a loose hourly, daily, weekly or monthly cycle with no cron syntax, so exact schedules mean running a scheduler like Supercronic yourself.


### 4. Northflank


Northflank is a container platform that runs services, jobs and databases either on its own managed cloud or inside your own cloud account.


**Best for:** teams that want PaaS ergonomics now and the option to run in their own AWS, Google Cloud or Azure account later.


**Pricing:** a free Sandbox covers two services, two jobs and one database, and doesn't sleep. Pay as you go is billed per second with no seat fees, with plans from about $2.70 a month for 0.1 vCPU and 256 MB and $12 for 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB, and egress is $0.06 per GB.


**Databases:** managed addons for Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and RabbitMQ, with automatic failover for Postgres and MongoDB. Scheduled work runs as jobs with a standard crontab.


**Regions:** 17 on Northflank's managed cloud, including Canada, Zurich and South Africa, or any region of a cloud you bring, with AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle and CoreWeave listed for bring-your-own-cloud.


**Tradeoff:** there are more concepts to learn than on Render, such as addons, secret groups and BYOC clusters, which pays off at scale and slows down a first deploy.


### 5. Heroku


Heroku is one of the original Git-push platforms, and it runs apps on AWS infrastructure that Heroku manages.


**Best for:** teams that want a mature, well-documented platform with a large add-on marketplace.


**Pricing:** the Eco plan is $5 a month for a shared pool of dyno hours, and Eco dynos sleep after 30 minutes of inactivity. Basic dynos are $7 and stay on, and Standard-1X dynos are $25.


**Databases:** Heroku Postgres starts at $5 a month for Essential-0 and $50 for Standard-0, and Heroku Key-Value Store starts at $3. The Scheduler add-on runs jobs every 10 minutes, hourly or daily, and Heroku describes its runs as expected but not guaranteed.


**Regions:** Common Runtime apps run in the US or Europe, and Private Spaces add ten regions, including Montreal, Sydney and Tokyo.


**Tradeoff:** in February 2026, Heroku[moved to a sustaining engineering model](https://www.heroku.com/blog/an-update-on-heroku/) focused on stability, security and support, and stopped offering Enterprise contracts to new customers. Existing apps keep running and card-paying customers can still sign up, but new features are no longer the focus.


### 6. DigitalOcean App Platform


App Platform is DigitalOcean's managed PaaS. It builds from a repo or container image and runs web services, workers and jobs next to DigitalOcean's managed databases.


**Best for:** teams already on DigitalOcean, or those who want simple flat pricing.


**Pricing:** up to three static-site apps are free. The smallest container is $5 a month with 512 MiB of memory and 50 GiB of transfer, and extra transfer is $0.02 per GiB.


**Databases:** a development Postgres database costs $7 a month, is not backed up by default and is deleted with the app. Managed Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB and Valkey start at about $15 a month, and managed Postgres can restore to any point in the last seven days. Scheduled jobs use a cron expression with a time zone, run at most every 15 minutes and are billed only while they run.


**Regions:** 12 for apps, including New York, San Francisco, Toronto, London, Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Bangalore, Singapore and Sydney.


**Tradeoff:** the $5 and $10 containers run as one fixed instance, and autoscaling on CPU needs dedicated-CPU instances, though autoscaling on request rate also works on shared plans.


### 7. Google Cloud Run


Cloud Run runs containers on Google Cloud and scales them with requests, down to zero when idle.


**Best for:** stateless APIs with uneven traffic on Google Cloud.


**Pricing:** with request-based billing, the first 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2 million requests each month are free. After that, instance time is billed while it handles requests, rounded up to the nearest 100 milliseconds.


**Databases:** Postgres comes from Cloud SQL and Redis from Memorystore, each set up and billed separately. The smallest Cloud SQL instance, db-f1-micro, is about $8 a month plus storage, and shared-core instances like it aren't covered by the Cloud SQL SLA. Scheduled work runs as Cloud Run jobs triggered by Cloud Scheduler.


**Regions:** Google Cloud regions across the world.


**Tradeoff:** you put the pieces together yourself in Google Cloud, including networking and IAM, so a multi-service app takes more setup than on Render.


### 8. AWS with ECS Express Mode


If the reason you are leaving Render is that you need AWS in your own account, the closest native service is ECS Express Mode. You give it a container image, a task execution role and an infrastructure role, and it creates a Fargate service behind a load balancer with HTTPS, autoscaling and a URL. AWS App Runner, the older option,[stopped accepting new customers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apprunner/latest/relnotes/relnotes.html) on April 30, 2026, and AWS recommends Express Mode in its place.


**Best for:** teams with AWS experience that want full control in their own account.


**Pricing:** Express Mode itself has no extra charge, and you pay for the resources it creates. A small app with one Fargate task (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB), a load balancer and the smallest RDS Postgres instance comes to about $60 a month in us-east-1, before logs and data transfer. Express services with the same network setup share a load balancer, which helps when you run several.


**Databases:** Postgres and MySQL on RDS, Redis-compatible Valkey on ElastiCache, and cron jobs through EventBridge Scheduler running ECS tasks.


**Regions:** nearly every AWS region.


**Tradeoff:** you own the operating, from networking and IAM to alarms and on-call, and the database and scheduler are separate services to configure. Our[Railway to AWS guide](https://modelence.com/migrate/railway-to-aws) maps each piece of a similar stack to its AWS service, and most of it applies to a Render app too.


### 9. Coolify


Coolify is an open-source, self-hostable PaaS that deploys apps, databases and one-click services to servers you control.


**Best for:** teams that want Render-style deploys on their own VPS or bare metal, at server cost.


**Pricing:** self-hosting is free, and Coolify Cloud, which hosts the dashboard for you, is $5 a month for two servers plus $3 for each extra server.


**Databases:** Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, Redis and a few other engines run as containers on your server. Scheduled backups to S3-compatible storage cover most of them, though not Redis. Scheduled tasks use cron expressions.


**Regions:** wherever your servers are.


**Tradeoff:** you are responsible for the servers, including OS updates and database failover, and for recovering when a machine goes down.


## Render vs Railway vs Fly.io


### Render vs Railway


Both run services, workers, cron jobs and databases from a repo, and the main difference is how you pay. Render charges a fixed monthly price per compute plan, while Railway bills the CPU and memory your app uses each second, so a steadily busy app is easier to budget on Render and a quiet one is often cheaper on Railway. Render autoscales on CPU and memory on Pro and up, while Railway runs the replica count you set. The[full Railway vs Render comparison](https://modelence.com/compare/railway-vs-render) works through what a web service, a worker and a small Postgres cost on each.


### Render vs Fly.io


Render is built for getting a multi-service app running quickly in one of five regions, while Fly.io is built for placing small Machines close to users in regions on six continents. Fly.io asks for more infrastructure knowledge, and its cheapest Postgres plan pauses when idle, so a single-region app with a database is usually simpler on Render, and a global app gets more control on Fly.io.


## How to choose a Render alternative


Start from the reason you are leaving, since each one points to a different platform:


- **You want the same workflow with usage-based billing:** Railway, or DigitalOcean App Platform if you are already on DigitalOcean.
- **You need regions Render doesn't have:** Modelence and Northflank for 17 regions each, or Fly.io for placing the app close to users worldwide.
- **Your customers expect AWS:** Modelence if you want AWS without running it yourself, ECS Express Mode if you have the team to operate AWS directly, or Northflank BYOC in your own account.
- **You want lower costs and have ops experience:** Coolify on your own servers, or Cloud Run if your traffic is bursty.
- **You don't want to be on call:** pick a platform that operates the app after the deploy, which is what Modelence's production autopilot does on Pro and above.


Before you commit, map last month's Render usage onto each candidate's instance sizes and database plans, since database pricing and bandwidth are where totals differ most.


## How to migrate off Render


A Render project moves in roughly the same steps wherever it is going:


1. **List your services and variables.** If you use a` render.yaml` Blueprint, it already lists your web services, private services, workers, cron jobs and environment groups. Otherwise, go through the dashboard and note each service's build and start commands, instance size and environment variables, including the ones that come from environment groups.
2. **Recreate the services.** Each Render service becomes a service on the new platform, built from its Dockerfile or the same build and start commands. Cron jobs become cron jobs or timers inside a running service, and files on a persistent disk move to object storage such as S3.
3. **Copy the data.** For a small database, a` pg_dump` and` pg_restore` during a short write pause is the simplest route. To keep the app serving while data copies, use logical replication: on Render it needs a Pro workspace or higher, a database with at least 10 GB of storage and a request to Render support to turn it on. Key Value data used as a cache can simply warm up again on the new platform.
4. **Switch over.** When the new database has caught up, stop writes on Render and copy the sequence values, which replication doesn't carry. Then point your domain at the new app.


On Modelence, your coding agent does most of this: it reads your project, writes the config file with your services and databases, and runs the deploy, and you add the secrets in the browser. The[Railway migration guide](https://modelence.com/migrate/railway) shows that flow step by step, from listing services to moving the domain.


## Frequently asked questions (FAQs)


What is the best alternative to Render?


Railway is the closest like-for-like replacement, since it runs the same mix of web services, workers, cron jobs and databases from a repo, and bills by usage instead of by instance size. If you need your app on AWS in a specific region with the operating handled for you, Modelence is the better fit. Fly.io suits apps that need to run close to users in many regions.


Is Railway cheaper than Render?


It depends on how busy your app is. Railway bills CPU and memory by the second as they are used, so a mostly idle app can cost very little, while Render charges a fixed price per compute plan, starting at $7 a month for 0.5 CPU and 512 MB. Steady, busy apps are often cheaper and easier to forecast on Render, while bandwidth-heavy apps pay less on Railway, at $0.05 per GB against Render's $0.15 beyond the plan allowance.


Which Render alternatives have more regions?


Render runs in five regions: Oregon, Ohio, Virginia, Frankfurt and Singapore. Modelence runs in 17 AWS regions, including Montreal, London, São Paulo, Tokyo and Sydney, Northflank in 17 regions on its managed cloud or any region of your own cloud, and Fly.io in regions on six continents.


Is there a free alternative to Render?


Several have free options. Modelence is free for hobby projects, Northflank's Sandbox covers two services, two jobs and a database, new Fly.io accounts start on a Free plan that covers $5 of usage a month once a card is added, Google Cloud Run has a monthly free tier, and Coolify is free to self-host on your own servers.


Can I run a Render-style app on AWS?


Yes. The closest native AWS option is ECS Express Mode, which turns a container image into a Fargate service with a load balancer, HTTPS and autoscaling, with databases on RDS and ElastiCache. Modelence also runs your services and databases on AWS, from one config file your coding agent writes, and keeps operating them after the deploy.


Which Render alternatives offer a HIPAA BAA?


Render signs a BAA on its Scale and Enterprise plans, with a 20% fee on all usage. Modelence signs BAAs on the Enterprise plan, and Railway signs one as an add-on for Pro workspaces with at least $1,000 a month of committed spend.


How do I migrate from Render without downtime?


Deploy the app on the new platform first, then copy your Postgres data with logical replication while the Render app keeps serving. On Render, logical replication needs a Pro workspace or higher, a database with at least 10 GB of storage and a request to Render support. When the new database has caught up, stop writes on Render, copy the sequence values and move your domain, so the only pause is the switch itself.
